rule.summary: Training status is judged by how fast you progress, not by years or strength: novices improve almost every session, intermediates week to week, advanced lifters month to month.

output.why: Training status is judged by how fast you progress, not by years or strength: novices improve almost every session, intermediates week to week, advanced lifters month to month.

rule.summary: If you are unsure of your status: under a year of consistent training counts as novice; 5+ years with heavy lifts that barely move month to month counts as advanced; otherwise intermediate.

output.why: If you are unsure of your status: under a year of consistent training counts as novice; 5+ years with heavy lifts that barely move month to month counts as advanced; otherwise intermediate.

rule.summary: After 8+ weeks of logs the app checks how often your anchor lifts improve and suggests a status change if your logs disagree with your setting twice in a row.

output.why: After 8+ weeks of logs the app checks how often your anchor lifts improve and suggests a status change if your logs disagree with your setting twice in a row.

rule.summary: Status can differ between body regions. The app stores one status for now.

output.why: Status can differ between body regions. The app stores one status for now.

rule.summary: When you lift and play a sport, one has to come first. If the sport comes first, lifting stays lower in volume, further from failure and avoids risky exercises and heavy soreness.

output.why: When you lift and play a sport, one has to come first. If the sport comes first, lifting stays lower in volume, further from failure and avoids risky exercises and heavy soreness.

rule.summary: About 4 hard sets per muscle per week is the minimum that reliably grows muscle. Targets never go below this.

output.why: Below about 4 hard sets a week a muscle barely grows, so no target goes lower.

rule.summary: For most people 10–20 hard sets per muscle per week is the practical range; more is reserved for specialisation phases.

output.why: Most people grow best somewhere between 10 and 20 hard sets per muscle each week.

rule.summary: Extra sets give smaller and smaller returns around 30 per week, so 30 is the hard ceiling for a specialised muscle.

output.why: Extra sets give smaller and smaller returns around 30 per week, so 30 is the hard ceiling for a specialised muscle.

rule.summary: More weekly sets cost more time: roughly 4–8 sets per muscle ≈ 1–2.5 h/week, up to 9+ h/week at 21–30 sets. Fewer sets give more growth per set.

output.why: More weekly sets cost more time: roughly 4–8 sets per muscle ≈ 1–2.5 h/week, up to 9+ h/week at 21–30 sets. Fewer sets give more growth per set.

rule.summary: Sets are counted fractionally: 1 set for each muscle an exercise mainly trains and half a set for each muscle it trains secondarily.

output.why: Compound lifts count fully for the main muscles and half for the helpers; that is how the body map adds up sets.

rule.summary: A set only counts toward muscle growth if it has at least 4 reps and ends within about 4 reps of failure. Warm-ups never count.

output.why: A set only counts toward muscle growth if it has at least 4 reps and ends within about 4 reps of failure. Warm-ups never count.

rule.summary: Start with the least volume that still drives progress and add sets only after a real plateau with good recovery.

output.why: You start with the least volume that should work; more is added only if you stall while recovering well.

rule.summary: Advanced lifters can specialise: raise 1–2 muscles by about half and cut the rest by a third to a half for 8–12 weeks, then return to a balanced phase.

output.why: Advanced lifters can specialise: raise 1–2 muscles by about half and cut the rest by a third to a half for 8–12 weeks, then return to a balanced phase.

rule.summary: Keep any single session at or below about 11 sets for one muscle; spread more volume over more sessions.

output.why: Past roughly 11 sets for one muscle in one session, extra sets are mostly junk, so volume is split across days.

rule.summary: Weekly sets set the frequency: 4–10 sets → 1–2 sessions per week, 11–20 → 2–3, 21–30 → 3 or more.

output.why: Weekly sets set the frequency: 4–10 sets → 1–2 sessions per week, 11–20 → 2–3, 21–30 → 3 or more.

rule.summary: For strength, train each main lift 2–6 times a week with 1–2 direct sets per session, spread over as many sessions as possible.

output.why: For strength, train each main lift 2–6 times a week with 1–2 direct sets per session, spread over as many sessions as possible.

rule.summary: Three to five lifting days with each muscle trained 2–4 times a week suits most lifters. Two days is the minimum and fine for maintenance.

output.why: Three to five lifting days with each muscle trained 2–4 times a week suits most lifters. Two days is the minimum and fine for maintenance.

rule.summary: The app picks the fewest lifting days that keep every session within your time limit and every muscle at a workable frequency.

output.why: The app chose the fewest lifting days that keep sessions within your time limit.

rule.summary: Keep at least one full rest day per week with no lifting and no hard sport.

output.why: Keep at least one full rest day per week with no lifting and no hard sport.

rule.summary: Cardio interferes least with lifting when done after lifting, at least 3 hours apart, or best of all on a different day.

output.why: Cardio interferes least with lifting when done after lifting, at least 3 hours apart, or best of all on a different day.

rule.summary: Avoid hard leg sessions within about 24 hours before a leg-heavy match or hard session, and the day after a match.

output.why: Heavy legs right before a match or the day after one hurts both, so leg days were moved away from matches.

rule.summary: Avoid lots of work for a muscle the day before a main lift that relies on it (for example heavy quad work the day before squats).

output.why: Avoid lots of work for a muscle the day before a main lift that relies on it (for example heavy quad work the day before squats).

rule.summary: Back-to-back hard days happen; on the second day simply expect to use a bit less load.

output.why: Back-to-back hard days happen; on the second day simply expect to use a bit less load.

rule.summary: Choose a split that keeps sessions practical and no muscle above about 11 sets per session; higher weekly volume needs more frequency.

output.why: Choose a split that keeps sessions practical and no muscle above about 11 sets per session; higher weekly volume needs more frequency.

rule.summary: Lower-body sessions are the most draining, so when leg volume is high, spread it over more days.

output.why: Lower-body sessions are the most draining, so when leg volume is high, spread it over more days.

rule.summary: Use 1–3 exercises per main movement and cover the gaps: an incline press, a wide-elbow row and a lat-focused pull, plus isolation for quads, hamstrings, biceps, triceps, side delts and calves.

output.why: Use 1–3 exercises per main movement and cover the gaps: an incline press, a wide-elbow row and a lat-focused pull, plus isolation for quads, hamstrings, biceps, triceps, side delts and calves.

rule.summary: An exercise must actually train the muscle it is meant to grow.

output.why: An exercise must actually train the muscle it is meant to grow.

rule.summary: When options are otherwise equal, prefer exercises that load the muscle hard in its stretched position.

output.why: When options are otherwise equal, prefer exercises that load the muscle hard in its stretched position.

rule.summary: Exercises must be practical: available equipment, no injury conflict, something you do not hate, quick to set up.

output.why: Exercises must be practical: available equipment, no injury conflict, something you do not hate, quick to set up.

rule.summary: Order sessions with free-weight compounds first, machines next and isolation last, unless a lagging muscle needs priority.

output.why: Order sessions with free-weight compounds first, machines next and isolation last, unless a lagging muscle needs priority.

rule.summary: Keep the same exercises for a whole block so progress is measurable; change only one or two per session between blocks.

output.why: Keep the same exercises for a whole block so progress is measurable; change only one or two per session between blocks.

rule.summary: For strength, the main lifts provide their own volume; extra muscle work uses quicker, less fatiguing exercises.

output.why: For strength, the main lifts provide their own volume; extra muscle work uses quicker, less fatiguing exercises.

rule.summary: Work around pain: drop exercises that load a painful area heavily, favour machines and higher reps, and see a professional for persistent or red-flag pain.

output.why: Work around pain: drop exercises that load a painful area heavily, favour machines and higher reps, and see a professional for persistent or red-flag pain.

rule.summary: Muscle grows from roughly 4–30 rep loads when sets end close to failure; the lower the reps, the more reps you can leave in the tank. Strength needs heavy loads (1–8 reps).

output.why: Muscle grows from roughly 4–30 rep loads when sets end close to failure; the lower the reps, the more reps you can leave in the tank. Strength needs heavy loads (1–8 reps).

rule.summary: Hypertrophy sets need at least 4 reps. Avoid going to complete failure on free-weight squats, hinges and presses.

output.why: Hypertrophy sets need at least 4 reps. Avoid going to complete failure on free-weight squats, hinges and presses.

rule.summary: Each exercise type has its own rep and effort range: heavy lower-body free weights 4–8 reps at 2–4 RIR, presses and leg machines 4–12, machines and rows 6–15, isolation 8–20 close to failure.

output.why: Big free-weight lifts stay a few reps short of failure; machines and isolation can go closer.

rule.summary: Vary rep ranges (within a session, between sessions or between weeks), but do not spend more than about 3 weeks outside hypertrophy ranges.

output.why: Mixing heavier and lighter rep ranges covers more ground for growth than always doing the same reps.

rule.summary: When your sport comes first, every lifting set stops one rep further from failure and the heaviest rep range on leg compounds is dropped.

output.why: When your sport comes first, every lifting set stops one rep further from failure and the heaviest rep range on leg compounds is dropped.

rule.summary: RPE 10 = 0 reps in reserve, 9 = 1, 8 = 2, 7 = 3. Most people underestimate how many reps they have left by about one, especially on high-rep sets.

output.why: Most people have about one more rep in them than they think, especially on high-rep sets.

rule.summary: For strength main lifts rest until ready: at least 2 minutes, usually about 3.

output.why: For strength main lifts rest until ready: at least 2 minutes, usually about 3.

rule.summary: For hypertrophy rest at least 90 seconds on average; longer for big lower-body lifts.

output.why: For hypertrophy rest at least 90 seconds on average; longer for big lower-body lifts.

rule.summary: Supersets and drop sets save time; a four-drop drop set counts as about three normal sets.

output.why: Supersets and drop sets save time; a four-drop drop set counts as about three normal sets.

rule.summary: Lower the weight under control in about 1–4 seconds and lift with intent; any lifting speed works as long as the set gets close to failure.

output.why: Lower the weight under control in about 1–4 seconds and lift with intent; any lifting speed works as long as the set gets close to failure.

rule.summary: Warm up generally, then ramp up on the first compound. Dynamic stretching is fine; keep static stretching brief for muscles you are about to train.

output.why: Warm up generally, then ramp up on the first compound. Dynamic stretching is fine; keep static stretching brief for muscles you are about to train.

rule.summary: Pick a first-set load that lands in the rep range at the top of the RIR range and stop the set there.

output.why: Pick a first-set weight that lands in the range while leaving the top-of-range reps in reserve.

rule.summary: If the first set lands in range, keep the load for the remaining sets and aim for the same reps. Reps falling on later sets is fine.

output.why: Your first set landed in range: keep the weight and aim to match those reps.

rule.summary: If the first set misses the rep range, change the load by about 4% per rep you missed or exceeded and keep that load for the rest of the sets.

output.why: Your first set missed the range, so the weight moved about 4% for every rep you were off.

rule.summary: When the first set hits the top of the rep range at the top of the RIR range, add load next session.

output.why: You hit the top of the rep range with reps to spare: time to add weight.

rule.summary: Session-to-session swings are normal. On a strong day you can jump ahead; on a flat day drop a step and chase reps.

output.why: Session-to-session swings are normal. On a strong day you can jump ahead; on a flat day drop a step and chase reps.

rule.summary: Typical pace: novices add load every 2–3 sessions, intermediates about every 5, advanced lifters about half as often.

output.why: Typical pace: novices add load every 2–3 sessions, intermediates about every 5, advanced lifters about half as often.

rule.summary: Strength training cycles a Volume phase and a Load phase (and a Peak phase before a test), with an easier intro week when coming back to volume.

output.why: Strength training cycles a Volume phase and a Load phase (and a Peak phase before a test), with an easier intro week when coming back to volume.

rule.summary: Volume phase: 1–3 top singles per lift per week getting harder (RPE 5 → 8), then normal working sets; 10–20 weekly sets for the supporting muscles.

output.why: Volume phase: 1–3 top singles per lift per week getting harder (RPE 5 → 8), then normal working sets; 10–20 weekly sets for the supporting muscles.

rule.summary: Load phase: 2–4 singles per lift per week (RPE 6 → 9), each followed by 2 back-off sets of 5 → 3 reps; supporting volume drops to 5–10 sets.

output.why: Load phase: 2–4 singles per lift per week (RPE 6 → 9), each followed by 2 back-off sets of 5 → 3 reps; supporting volume drops to 5–10 sets.

rule.summary: Peak phase (only before a test): heavy singles up to RPE 10, few back-off sets and very little extra volume for 2–4 weeks.

output.why: Peak phase (only before a test): heavy singles up to RPE 10, few back-off sets and very little extra volume for 2–4 weeks.

rule.summary: Estimated 1-rep max (e1RM) uses a Brzycki-style formula on effective reps (reps + RIR): load × 36 ÷ (37 − effective reps). Sets above 12 effective reps are too far from a max to estimate, so they are left out.

output.why: Estimated 1-rep max (e1RM) uses a Brzycki-style formula on effective reps (reps + RIR): load × 36 ÷ (37 − effective reps). Sets above 12 effective reps are too far from a max to estimate, so they are left out.

rule.summary: Train each main lift 2–4 times a week; a session that works the same muscles with another lift counts as half an exposure.

output.why: Train each main lift 2–4 times a week; a session that works the same muscles with another lift counts as half an exposure.

rule.summary: Each week answer five quick recovery questions. Two or more “yes” answers means a deload next week.

output.why: Two or more “yes” answers in the weekly check means fatigue is building; a lighter week helps you bounce back.

rule.summary: Deloads happen when you need them, not on a fixed calendar.

output.why: Deloads happen when you need them, not on a fixed calendar.

rule.summary: A standard deload cuts sets on every exercise by about 30–50% while keeping loads, effort and number of sessions.

output.why: A deload keeps the weights and effort but cuts sets, so you recover without losing strength.

rule.summary: If only one area is beaten up, deload just that area: drop or reduce the exercises that load it and train everything else normally.

output.why: If only one area is beaten up, deload just that area: drop or reduce the exercises that load it and train everything else normally.

rule.summary: If aches flare with heavy loads but not with high reps, use a week of higher reps on those exercises.

output.why: If aches flare with heavy loads but not with high reps, use a week of higher reps on those exercises.

rule.summary: After a big volume jump, time off, or moving from heavy work back to volume, run the first week at about 75% of the sets and one rep further from failure.

output.why: Jumping straight into a lot more volume makes you very sore; an easier first week avoids that.

rule.summary: Missed a session? Move it to the next free day, never stack two missed hard sessions on one day, and drop the least important one if the week runs out.

output.why: Missed a session? Move it to the next free day, never stack two missed hard sessions on one day, and drop the least important one if the week runs out.

rule.summary: Feeling drained? Swap today for the lightest session of the week.

output.why: Feeling drained? Swap today for the lightest session of the week.

rule.summary: Every sport session at moderate effort or harder counts as one hard session in your weekly load.

output.why: Every sport session at moderate effort or harder counts as one hard session in your weekly load.

rule.summary: Each weekly sport session trims lifting volume for the muscles that sport works hardest: 0.5–1.5 sets per session, at most 4 per muscle, never below 4 sets.

output.why: Your sport already works these muscles, so lifting volume for them is trimmed to protect recovery.

rule.summary: Sport days are fixed; lifting days move around them using the scheduling rules.

output.why: Sport days are fixed; lifting days move around them using the scheduling rules.

rule.summary: Extra conditioning should be low-impact (bike, rower, swimming), short and hard or under an hour, after lifting or on other days.

output.why: Extra conditioning should be low-impact (bike, rower, swimming), short and hard or under an hour, after lifting or on other days.

rule.summary: When the sport comes first, leg muscles are capped at 8 sets, sets stop further from failure and high-risk lifts are avoided.

output.why: When the sport comes first, leg muscles are capped at 8 sets, sets stop further from failure and high-risk lifts are avoided.

rule.summary: Energy burned in sports is added to your calorie target.

output.why: Energy burned in sports is added to your calorie target.

rule.summary: Your nutrition phase follows your goal (gain, maintain or lose) and you can override it.

output.why: Your nutrition phase follows your goal (gain, maintain or lose) and you can override it.

rule.summary: Spend at least four times as long gaining or maintaining as cutting.

output.why: Spend at least four times as long gaining or maintaining as cutting.

rule.summary: Muscle can be built at maintenance or in a small deficit, especially by newer lifters; higher body fat does not stop gains.

output.why: Muscle can be built at maintenance or in a small deficit, especially by newer lifters; higher body fat does not stop gains.

rule.summary: Resting energy use is roughly 22 kcal per kg of bodyweight per day.

output.why: Resting energy use is roughly 22 kcal per kg of bodyweight per day.

rule.summary: Multiply by an activity factor for lifters: sedentary 1.3–1.6, lightly active 1.5–1.8, active 1.7–2.0, very active 1.9–2.2.

output.why: Multiply by an activity factor for lifters: sedentary 1.3–1.6, lightly active 1.5–1.8, active 1.7–2.0, very active 1.9–2.2.

rule.summary: Any maintenance estimate is rough; adjusting from your weight trend is what makes it accurate.

output.why: Every calorie formula is a guess; your weight trend over the next weeks corrects it.

rule.summary: Your lifestyle factor excludes sports; those are added separately so they are not counted twice.

output.why: Your lifestyle factor excludes sports; those are added separately so they are not counted twice.

rule.summary: Lose 0.5–1% of bodyweight per week; leaner people should stay near 0.5%.

output.why: Lose 0.5–1% of bodyweight per week; leaner people should stay near 0.5%.

rule.summary: Gain per month: novices 1–2% of bodyweight, intermediates 0.5–1.5%, advanced up to 0.5%.

output.why: Gain per month: novices 1–2% of bodyweight, intermediates 0.5–1.5%, advanced up to 0.5%.

rule.summary: About 7,700 kcal per kg of bodyweight change, so the daily calorie change ≈ weekly kg change × 1,100.

output.why: About 7,700 kcal per kg of bodyweight change, so the daily calorie change ≈ weekly kg change × 1,100.

rule.summary: Deficits much bigger than 500 kcal/day cost more muscle; the app warns above 750.

output.why: Deficits much bigger than 500 kcal/day cost more muscle; the app warns above 750.

rule.summary: Extra energy per 10 minutes of activity: light ≈ 0.44 kcal/kg, moderate ≈ 0.99, vigorous ≈ 1.54. Watches usually overestimate.

output.why: Extra energy per 10 minutes of activity: light ≈ 0.44 kcal/kg, moderate ≈ 0.99, vigorous ≈ 1.54. Watches usually overestimate.

rule.summary: Sport intensity maps to cardio intensity: light → light, moderate → moderate, hard → vigorous, match → between moderate and vigorous.

output.why: Sport intensity maps to cardio intensity: light → light, moderate → moderate, hard → vigorous, match → between moderate and vigorous.

rule.summary: Sport calories are averaged over the week and added to every day.

output.why: Sport calories are averaged over the week and added to every day.

rule.summary: Eat at least 1.6 g of protein per kg of bodyweight when gaining or maintaining.

output.why: Eat at least 1.6 g of protein per kg of bodyweight when gaining or maintaining.

rule.summary: In a deficit, lean people (or anyone with unknown body fat) should eat at least 2.0 g/kg.

output.why: In a deficit, lean people (or anyone with unknown body fat) should eat at least 2.0 g/kg.

rule.summary: Eat at least 40–60 g of fat per day depending on size; around a quarter of maintenance calories is a good default.

output.why: Eat at least 40–60 g of fat per day depending on size; around a quarter of maintenance calories is a good default.

rule.summary: Eat at least 2 g/kg of carbohydrate when gaining or maintaining and at least 1 g/kg in a deficit.

rule.summary: Set protein first, then fat, then fill the rest of your calories with carbohydrate.

output.why: Set protein first, then fat, then fill the rest of your calories with carbohydrate.

rule.summary: Weigh in the morning after the bathroom and before eating. Daily swings of 1–2% are normal.

output.why: Weigh in the morning after the bathroom and before eating. Daily swings of 1–2% are normal.

rule.summary: Use the weekly average. A week needs at least 3 weigh-ins including a weekend day to be trusted.

rule.summary: A 14–21-day running average shows the long-term trend.

output.why: A 14–21-day running average shows the long-term trend.

rule.summary: Ignore the first week of a new gain or loss phase for rate decisions: water and food volume shift.

rule.summary: If weight did not move in the right direction in week one of a phase, adjust the activity factor by 0.2.

rule.summary: Wait at least 2 weeks after a calorie change before changing again.

rule.summary: Calorie cuts come from carbs and fat; protein stays the same.

output.why: Calorie cuts come from carbs and fat; protein stays the same.

rule.summary: A stalled cut can also be fixed with about 2,500 more steps a day or a few short cardio sessions, kept apart from lifting.

rule.summary: At maintenance, if weight drifts more than 0.25% per week over 3 weeks, adjust by 100–150 kcal.
